summary: Discusses desired enhancements to the naming architecture of GSS-API version 3, which authenticates named parties and lets names be used in access control lists. Newer security mechanisms and uses call for richer name handling.

plainLanguage.summary: Security systems check a person's name before letting them in. This note lists ways the naming rules could be improved so modern systems can describe who is who more fully.

questions: why are names unstable on access control lists
how should gss-api handle group membership
subtitle: Enhancements to the naming and authorization architecture of GSS-API.

tldr.problem: GSS-API stores names on access control lists (ACLs) to make authorization decisions, but names change over time (when people move in an organization or change names) and can be reused for different entities, making ACLs unstable. Additionally, some security mechanisms like public-key systems do not have a single canonical name, and Kerberos needs to include group or role information in authorization decisions.
tldr.mechanism: GSS-API Version 3 should support name attributes (properties of a name like group membership), alternate naming schemes, and mechanisms that allow multiple representations of the same identity, so authorization decisions can use more stable identifiers or richer context beyond just a single name string.
tldr.outcome: Systems can maintain more stable access control lists, support a wider range of security mechanisms, and make authorization decisions based on attributes and roles in addition to principal names.

facts.label: Proposed solution
facts.value: Name attributes and multiple name representations

today: RFC 4768 is an Informational RFC documenting desired enhancements for GSS-API Version 3. These naming and authorization enhancements remain relevant for systems that need to support diverse security mechanisms and attribute-based access control, particularly in organizations using Kerberos with group memberships or public-key systems with role information.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 4768 discusses desired enhancements to the naming architecture of the Generic Security Services Application Program Interface (GSS-API), focusing on how names are used in authentication and authorization. GSS-API is a standardized interface that allows applications to request authentication services from different underlying security mechanisms (like Kerberos or public-key cryptography) without knowing the details of each mechanism.

Traditionally, GSS-API treats names as single canonical strings that can be exported and stored in Access Control Lists (ACLs) for authorization decisions. However, advances in security mechanisms and the way organizations wish to use security systems require this model to be extended. The document motivates the need for extensions and describes solutions under discussion for GSS-API Version 3.
sections.plainLanguage: When systems prove who someone is, they use names. But names are not always stable or complete. This document explains why that is a problem and how to fix it.

sections.title: The Name Stability Problem
sections.content:
A fundamental issue with storing names on ACLs is that names change over time. If a name includes organizational information (such as a domain or department affiliation), it becomes invalid when the person moves to a different part of the organization. Even without organizational information, people change their names, and updating all ACLs to reflect these changes is administratively burdensome.

A more serious problem is name reuse. If a Unix user account is deleted and the same user ID is later assigned to a different person, that new person automatically inherits the old user's privileges from the ACL. This is a security vulnerability. The RFC motivates the need for more stable identifiers that do not change when a person's organizational role or legal name changes, and that cannot be reused to refer to a different entity.
sections.plainLanguage: If you write someone's name on the door list and they move departments, you have to update it. Worse, if their name is reused for someone new, that new person can pretend to be the old person.

sections.title: Kerberos and Enterprise Names
sections.content:
Kerberos, one of the most widely deployed security mechanisms, exemplifies these problems. Kerberos supports enterprise names, which are user-friendly aliases (like "alice@company.com") that remain constant even if the user's Kerberos principal name changes internally as they move through the organization. This solves the stability problem for users but creates a dilemma for GSS-API: should the exported name (used on ACLs) be based on the enterprise name or the principal name?

If the exported name is based on the enterprise name, it is more stable, but if the mapping from enterprise name to principal changes, the exported name becomes invalid, defeating the purpose. If the exported name is based on the principal name, ACL entries become invalid when the principal changes. Additionally, Kerberos authorization data can include group membership information that should be usable in authorization decisions, but GSS-API currently has no standard mechanism to expose this information to applications.
sections.plainLanguage: In Kerberos, your login name stays the same even if your real Kerberos name changes. But which one should go on the door list? And if you are in the "managers" group, how does the system know to let you in the managers-only room?

sections.title: Public-Key and X.509 Naming Challenges
sections.content:
Public-key mechanisms and X.509 certificates introduce different challenges. X.509 names are more complex than Kerberos names and often contain organizational information embedded in certificate fields (organization, department, country, etc.). When a person changes jobs, these fields may no longer be valid, but changing a certificate field is not straightforward.

More fundamentally, some public-key mechanisms do not have a single canonical name at all. A person might authenticate using different public keys in different contexts, or a key might be used across multiple organizational domains. The GSS-API requirement that any imported name can be canonicalized into a single form is too restrictive for these mechanisms. Solutions must allow mechanisms to export names in multiple formats, to indicate alternative identities, and to return name attributes (like group membership or role) alongside the primary name.
sections.plainLanguage: X.509 certificates have all kinds of information embedded in them (where you work, what department, what country). If you change jobs, the certificate is wrong. And some systems do not have one single name at all.

sections.title: Proposed Extensions for GSS-API v3
sections.content:
The RFC describes several proposed extensions. One solution is name attributes: mechanisms can return structured attributes attached to a name, such as group memberships, roles, or organizational affiliations, without requiring these to be encoded in the name string itself. Applications can then make authorization decisions based on these attributes ("allow if the group attribute is 'admin'") rather than storing entire names on ACLs.

Another proposal allows mechanisms to support multiple name representations: a single identity can be exported in different forms depending on the context or the application's needs. For Kerberos, this might mean exporting both the enterprise name (for ACL stability) and the principal name (for Kerberos-specific operations). Credentials can include information about source identity selection, allowing mechanisms to indicate which of several available identities should be used in a particular context.

These extensions maintain backward compatibility with GSS-API Version 2 while providing richer semantic capabilities for authorization and attribute-based access control.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of storing names, store what a person IS: their groups, roles, or a stable ID number. Different situations can use different names for the same person.

left.title: Name-based ACL
left.desc: Breaks when name changes; vulnerable to name reuse.

right.title: Attribute-based ACL
right.desc: More stable; supports roles and groups; handles multiple names for one identity.
